editor.editor_institution: Department of Family Medicine, Michigan State University

list.listitem: The causative agent of lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) serovars L1, L2, or L3. A

Fever, malaise, and proctocolitis are the most common presentation of LGV. Among heterosexuals, tender inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy are common. Among men who have sex with men (MSM), about 25% of cases of anorectal LGV infections are asymptomatic. C

Diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion, epidemiologic information, and a C. trachomatis Nuclear Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) at the symptomatic anatomic site, along with exclusion of other etiologies for proctocolitis; inguinal lymphadenopathy; or genital, oral, or rectal ulcers. C Alternative tests include culture on swabs from genital lesions, rectal specimens, and lymph node specimens or serology. LGV genotyping can be requested on chlamydia-positive samples.
Recommended treatment is doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 21 days. If allergic to tetracyclines or pregnant, use erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 21 days. B

Patients should be followed clinically for 3 to 6 weeks until signs and symptoms resolve. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (STI Treatment Guideline, 2021) recommends retesting for chlamydia approximately 3 months after LGV treatment. There is evidence of spontaneous remission in 8 weeks. B

background.definition: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) which causes systemic manifestations that can present as an inguinal syndrome, with genital ulceration and groin lymphadenopathy (buboes), or as an anogenitorectal syndrome with proctocolitis, fever, malaise, chills, anorexia, myalgia, and arthralgia. If left untreated, the infection can lead to fistula formation, genital elephantiasis, rectal strictures and infertility.

list.listitem: While LGV is uncommon, there have been recent outbreaks among men who have sex with men (MSM).

In one study of MSM, LGV was a cause of infectious proctitis in a significantly higher percentage of men who were human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-positive than HIV-negative (7.8% vs. 0.7%, respectively), although the 2021 European guideline notes that LGV proctitis is increasingly found in HIV-negative MSM. Other causes of infectious proctitis in this study included chlamydia (23.4% vs. 21.7%, respectively), gonorrhea (13.4% vs. 10.8%, respectively), HSV-1 (14.2% vs. 6.5%, respectively), and HSV-2 (22% vs. 12.3%, respectively). Multiple infections were seen significantly more often in HIV-positive MSM (17.7% vs. 8.6%, respectively).

In a study in an STI clinic in Belgium, more than half (56.2%) of LGV cases were found in HIV-negative men in 2019. In this study, introduction of PrEP did not appear to accelerate the increase in LGV cases, although LGV prevalence in the Antwerp male PrEP cohort increased from 0.8% in 2017 to 2.4% in 2019.
Among 224 patients with HIV in Switzerland who were seeking sexual healthcare, 0.9% (95%CI 0.1%, 6.2%) of MSM had laboratory-documented LVG compared to none of the heterosexual men or women.
The prevalence rate was higher at 9% in a case series of 713 MSM who were CT positive and receiving care in the UK.

In a surveillance study of New York City Sexual Health Clinics in which rectal CT testing was performed among MSM using NAAT, there were 114 LGV diagnoses among 1,317 tested specimens, for a positivity rate of 6.6% (2008) to 10.3% (2011).
Using 132 remnant C. trachomatis-positive rectal specimens collected from 7 US Public Health Laboratories, LGV-associated serovar L2 was identified in 14%.

In a 2017 French study of MSM who were using pre-exposure prophylaxis, a strain of genovar L was detected in 18.7% of cases. In an Italian study of 99 MSM who had a history of unsafe anal sexual intercourse, L2 CT genotype was identified in 13 rectal swabs.

In a recent European seroprevalence study using 500 chlamydia-positive rectal swabs from MSM, LGV positivity was 25.6% (95% CI 22.0%-29.6%) overall with a range of 47.6% in Austria to 14.4% in the UK.
Chlamydia trachomatis is a human pathogen and is the most common detected STI.

There are 15 serovars (subspecies, based on cell-surface antigens) within this species. Serovars A-C cause trachoma, serovars D-K cause genital tract infections, and serovars L-1 through L-3 are responsible for LGV.
The L-2 serovar can be further identified as L-2, L-2a, or L-2b on the basis of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequencing.

In a study of the molecular epidemiology of CT strains involved in LGV outbreaks in France, a change was noted from predominantly L2b until 2012 and L2 as the dominant strain starting in 2013. Also identified were 4 genetic L2b ompA variants.
A new LGV variant causing severe proctitis, designated L2c, has been reported that causes the vast majority of infections among MSM; it is also occasionally found among heterosexual women.

The causative agent of LGV, C. trachomatis serovars L1-L3, is a lymphotropic organism which initiates the disease process primarily in the lymphatic channels, leading to thrombolymphangitis with an extension of the inflammatory process to the draining lymph nodes.
Necrosis can occur with loculated abscesses, fistulas, and sinus tract formation.
Fibrosis replaces the acute inflammation with resulting obliteration of the lymphatic drainage, chronic edema, and stricture formation.
Inoculation site determines affected lymph nodes.
Urethral infection may be a reservoir for transmission. In a study of 341 MSM with anorectal LGV, 7 (2.1%) had concurrent urethral LGV. Four (6.8%) of 59 partners also had urethral LGV infection.
Pharyngeal infection can also occur. In a small case series of 4 MSM, LGV-associated CT DNA was detected from the pharynx.
In a case series of 26 MSM with symptomatic proctitis, 24 were HIV positive and all had LGV serovar L2 confirmed from rectal swabs. Coinfections with STIs were identified in 12 men.

list.listitem: Prevention is with condom use or abstinence; condom use does not always prevent transmission which can occur without penile penetration. C

Partners (those with whom the patient has had sexual contact within 60 days before symptom onset) of those infected with LGV should be evaluated and treated within 30 days of exposure. C The CDC (2021) recommends that asymptomatic partners be presumptively treated with a chlamydia regimen (doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 7 days). However, the 2019 European guideline on the management of LGV recommends treatment for 21 days for asymptomatic patients and contacts of patients with LGV OR obtaining a test of cure in those treated with other regimens.

Because LVG cases continue to occur primarily among MSM, most of whom are also HIV positive and co-infected with other STIs, screening these patients for gonorrhea, herpes simplex virus, and syphilis should be undertaken. C
Hepatitis C virus testing should also be offered to all patients with LGV. C
The secondary stage of LGV, which includes fever, malaise, painful inguinal buboes is the most common presentation. C
LGV can also present as an anogenitorectal syndrome with anal pruritus, rectal discharge, fever, rectal pain, constipation, tenesmus, thinning of stools, and weight loss. C

Diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion, epidemiologic information, and a C. trachomatis NAAT at the symptomatic anatomic site, along with exclusion of other etiologies for proctocolitis; inguinal lymphadenopathy; or genital, oral, or rectal ulcers. C
Alternative tests include culture or serology. LGV genotyping can be requested on chlamydia-positive samples. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Painful, tender, soft ulcer with exudate and tender inguinal adenopathy
Non-painful, non-tender, indurated ulcer without exudate, non-tender inguinal adenopathy
Painful, tender, soft ulcers with vesicles or pustules with or without inguinal adenopathy
Relatively painless ulcers with extensive granulation tissue base with sharply defined edges
Similar symptoms of proctitis, no genital ulcers, HIV-positive status favors LGV

list.listitem: LGV can manifest as an inguinal syndrome, with genital ulceration and groin lymphadenopathy (buboes) with subsequent suppuration. The initial lesion may go unnoticed and can be a localized inflamed papule or ulcer at the exposure site that is transient; the lesion occurs 3 to 30 days after inoculation.

In a surveillance study from New York City Sexual Health Clinics, among 295 MSM whose anorectal CT specimens were tested for LGV, 49 (16.6%) had LGV of whom 42 (86%) had anogenital signs and/or symptoms at the time of specimen collection and 7 (14%) were asymptomatic.

It has been reported that approximately 25% of LGV infections are asymptomatic, primarily among HIV-positive MSM. In an Australian study that began universal testing for LGV of all positive rectal C. trachomatis specimens in MSM over the age of 25 years, regardless of symptoms, significantly more asymptomatic cases were detected compared to the selective-testing period (34.4% (22/64) vs. 15.2% (5/33), respectively).

LGV can also manifest as an anogenitorectal syndrome, with proctocolitis and hyperplasia of intestinal and perirectal lymphatic tissue, most common with MSM. This presentation can be confused with inflammatory bowel disease. It is estimated that among MSM, the ratio of genital to anorectal LGV infections is 1:14.

Symptoms of proctitis include anorectal itching, pain, tenesmus (cramping), and discharge in and around the anal canal. In one study, tenesmus alone or in combination with constipation made a diagnosis of LGV more likely in MSM presenting with rectal symptoms.
Both syndromes can be accompanied by myalgia, arthralgia, fever, chills, and anorexia that occur 2 to 6 weeks after the primary lesion occurs; reactive arthropathy has been reported.
LGV has been reported to occur in orolabial and oropharyngeal sites and can involve cervical lymph nodes.

Diagnosis of LGV based on history and clinical presentation has been reported to be unreliable since symptoms may overlap with other genital ulcer diseases. Studies show that even experienced clinicians failed to achieve a correct clinical diagnosis in 22% to 50% of cases.
Findings on microscopy (e.g., polymorphonuclear cells) were not helpful for distinguishing NAAT positivity for a rectal STI in a study of 150 gay or bisexual men with proctitis.

Because chlamydia are intracellular organisms, specimens should be obtained from ulcer base exudate, rectal mucosa, aspirates of enlarged or fluctuant lymph nodes or buboes, aspirates using a <0.5 mL of a saline solution injected and re-aspirated for non-fluctuant nodes, or rectal and pharyngeal swabs from MSM and women exposed at those sites. A urethral swab or first-catch urine specimen can be used when urethritis and/or inguinal lymphadenopathy is present and LGV is suspected.

Genital lesions, rectal specimens, and lymph node specimens can be tested for C. trachomatis by culture, direct immunofluorescence, or nucleic acid detection. CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections guideline, 2021 recommends NAAT for C. trachomatis performed at the symptomatic anatomic site. The laboratory can be asked to perform LGV genotyping on chlamydia-positive samples.
The updated 2019 European guideline on LGV recommends testing for C. trachomatis with a commercial NAAT platform and confirming with an LGV discriminatory NAAT.

Two real-time PCR-based assays (Allplex Genital ulcer Assay and VIASURE) were found to be comparable for the detection of LGV in rectal samples, with positive percent agreement, negative percent agreement, and overall percent agreement of 88.9%, 100%, and 97.3%, and 91.6%, 100%, and 97.1%, respectively. These two assays were also found comparable to a single-plex assay RealCycler CHSL kit (Progenie Molecular) and another multiplex kit, the RealCycler Universal ULCGEN (Progenie Molecular), with overall agreement ranging between 91.3% and 100%.

Although serology can be used to support a diagnosis of LGV, serology tests for LGV are not standardized, have not been validated for presentations of proctocolitis, and also are not widely available. A microimmunofluorescence titer of >1:256 is suggestive of LGC.
The presence of rectal polymorphonuclear leucocytes from rectal swabs is predictive of LGV proctitis, especially in MSM who are HIV-positive.
It may be possible to identify Chlamydia trachomatis serovars using the fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) procedure.

In contrast to patients with inflammatory bowel disease, biopsy specimens from MSM with proctitis associated with LGV or syphilis showed minimal active chronic crypt centric damage; a lack of mucosal eosinophilia; and submucosal plasma cells, endothelial swelling, and perivascular plasma cells.

In a case report, a patient with an FDG PET/CT scan showing increased metabolic activity at the inguinal, iliac, and para-aortic lymph nodes suspicious for lymphoma was subsequently diagnosed with LGV.
Any patient who shows signs of ulceration anywhere on genital skin or mucosa should be evaluated for genital ulcer disease (GUD).
The importance of genital ulcers has increased considerably during the AIDS era, due to their apparent role in facilitating the transmission of HIV and other viruses.
Treatment of GUD can be based upon syndromic diagnosis of genital ulcer, presumptive clinical diagnosis, or microbiological/serological diagnosis.

Presumptive specific clinical diagnosis for GUD has previously been reported to be unreliable, as even experienced clinicians failed to achieve a correct clinic diagnosis in 22% and 50% of patients with GUD.
Consider testing for LVG in patients with C. trachomatis-positive rectal specimens, especially for MSM.
In patients with proven or suspected LVG, test for other potentially co-existing STIs, in particular gonorrhea, herpes simplex virus, and syphilis.
Cases of LVG should be reported to the health department.
First-line treatment is doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 21 days. B
Second-line treatment for patients allergic to tetracycline or who are pregnant is erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 21 days. B
Aspirate and drain buboes that are fluctuant. C
Recommended treatment: doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 21 days, tetracycline 2 g orally daily for 21 days.
Longer courses of therapy may be required in the setting of fistulas, buboes, and other forms of severe disease
Patients allergic to tetracycline should be treated with erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 21 days.
Azithromycin 1 g orally once a week for 3 weeks has shown effectiveness, however clinical trials are lacking.

In an open clinical trial of men who have sex with men (MSM) with LGV proctitis who received convenience allocation according to treating physician preferences, comparable cure rates were found for men treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days (41/43) and those treated with azithromycin 1 g orally once weekly for 3 weeks (80/82). Cure was defined as resolution of symptoms at week 6 with an additional supporting negative rectal PCR at week 4, if available.
Aspirate and drain buboes that are fluctuant.
Patients with fibrotic lesions or fistulas would be considered for reconstructive genital surgery.
Spontaneous remission can occur within 8 weeks.
Good to fair prognosis depending on the patient's immune system. C
Natural history is variable with spontaneous remission. C
Untreated LGV can result in fistulas, strictures and genital elephantiasis from lymphatic obstruction, and infertility. C
If left untreated, LGV can lead to lifelong disability and disfigurement to include fistulas, strictures, genital elephantiasis from lymphatic obstruction, and infertility.
LGV can facilitate the spread of HIV/AIDS if left untreated.

Reinfections occurred in 66 individuals (5.2%) of 1281 MSM who had a first LGV episode in a U.K. surveillance study. These patients were more likely to be HIV-positive, visit a London clinic, have hepatitis C or concurrent gonorrhea on their first-recorded LGV episode.
Symptoms should resolve within 1 to 2 weeks of commencing antibiotic therapy.
Patients should receive follow-up, usually for 3 to 6 weeks, until symptoms resolve.
Patients should be advised to avoid unprotected sexual intercourse until they and their partners(s) have completed treatment and follow-up.
CDC (2021) recommends retesting for chlamydia approximately 3 months after LGV treatment. They also suggest NAAT 4 weeks after completion of treatment when using an alternate regimen.
The 2019 European guidelines recommend a test of cure if using a treatment regimen other than doxycycline.
In one small case series, 3 of 4 MSM with LGV failed the 21-day doxycycline treatment.
Treatment for pregnant or lactating mothers should be with erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 21 days. Test of cure is advised at 4 weeks post-antibiotic treatment.
